A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same RAT+ research. Their main texts, equations, figures, tables and appendices are readable, and retained material can be matched despite substantial reorganization.

before.justification: v1 reports original pretraining, adaptation, downstream accuracy, ablation and efficiency experiments, including additional results in its appendices.

after.justification: v3 retains original experiments and adds 7.6B-model accuracy results, comparator evaluations and supplementary analyses.

M1.justification: The full-sequence recurrence and active recurrence learning architecture remain unchanged. v3 adds procedural variants: joint adaptation across seven dilations (Table 10) and combined top-k/dilated inference, attending fully within selected blocks and using compressed representations elsewhere (Table 19).

E1.justification: Both versions use FineWeb-Edu, PG19, the same six commonsense tasks, LongBench and RULER NIAH tasks. The PG19 experiment remains in v3 Table 11. Larger models and additional attention configurations do not introduce new dataset or task coverage.

E2.justification: v3 adds GQA/MQA comparisons (Figure 5), SnapKV and StreamingLLM to the NIAH comparison (Table 7), and Mamba2/GatedDeltaNet to the retained LongBench comparison (Table 5). Table 20 also introduces literature-reported Griffin/Pythia comparisons. Quest/MoBA comparisons already existed in v1.

E3.justification: v3 adds 7.6B-model training on 100B tokens, FLOPs-matched GQA/MQA configurations, a 1024-KV-entry NIAH comparison and a head-hit analysis over 500 examples. Appendix A.1 revises the reported smaller-model adaptation rate from an example of 2e-5 to 0.1 times the original learning rate, explicitly retaining earlier results; this does not establish rerunning them.

E4.justification: New analyses test whether recurrence improves block-selection hit rates (Table 9), whether one adaptation stage can cover multiple dilations (Table 10), whether positional encoding is necessary (Table 13), and whether dilation complements top-k attention (Table 19). Existing component, recurrence-placement and adaptation-curve analyses are retained.

E5.justification: Neither version reports experimental seed counts, repeated-run uncertainty, confidence intervals or significance tests. The new 500-example head analysis specifies a sample size, not uncertainty estimation.

E6.justification: v3 adds substantial comparator and analysis results, plus 7.6B accuracy results: Table 8 reports commonsense averages of 64.4 for dense inference and 63.1 at D=64. Earlier 1.5B and latency results are retained, while v1 Table 13's detailed 2.6B commonsense results disappear. New Table 9 reports attention accuracy of 57.4 where Table 17 retains 63.2 for the same stated NIAH-MK-2 setting, an unexplained mismatch.

T1.justification: The recurrence and dilated-attention equations and underlying mathematical formulation are retained. v3 adds empirical analyses and conceptual hypotheses, but no new formal assumptions, theorems, proofs or substantive mathematical derivations.

C1.justification: The central claims about dense pretraining enabling flexible sparse inference remain intact. The abstract and introduction extend the accuracy-scaling claim from 2.6B to 7.6B parameters and advertise approximately one point of accuracy loss with 64-fold attention FLOP and KV-cache reductions.

C2.justification: v3 adds hypotheses explaining NoPE performance through shorter effective attention spans and limited RepoBench scaling through insufficient code data. It qualifies multi-dilation adaptation by the enormous hybrid-configuration space and expands proposed byte-level and parallel-reasoning applications. The central recurrence and sparsification interpretations remain unchanged.

D1.justification: v3 supplies a code URL, documents the 7.6B model's dimensions and optimization hyperparameters, and clarifies adaptation learning rates in Appendix A.1. Conversely, it omits v1 Section 5.1's explicit instruction to always select the first and most recent blocks in top-k attention.

R1.justification: New Section 5.3 and Table 6 substantially expand positioning against GQA/MQA, KV-cache eviction and other efficiency approaches, distinguishing their computational, storage and access properties. Additional citations contextualize NoPE, retrieval heads and larger-model comparisons. The Rae/PG19 citation disappears although the PG19 experiment remains.

P1.justification: The introduction, contribution list and experimental narrative are extensively rewritten. Efficiency and top-k discussions are reordered, positioning receives its own subsection, and the former appendices B–D are consolidated into experimental subsections. Existing design explanations and adaptation discussion also move between the main text and appendix.

P2.justification: v3 adds the GQA/MQA plot and multiple comparison and analysis tables, expands the scaling plot with a 7.6B curve and attention reference markers, and adds baseline rows to Table 5. Adaptation curves move into the main text, retained appendix tables are rearranged and compacted, and the detailed 2.6B table is removed.

improvement.justification: v3 addresses important evaluation gaps: v1 provided 7B-scale throughput without corresponding accuracy evidence and lacked GQA/MQA and SnapKV comparisons. The new scaling results and controlled comparisons substantially strengthen support for the central efficiency–accuracy argument, while head-hit analysis tests the previously speculative block-scoring explanation. Removing detailed 2.6B results and introducing the unexplained Table 9/Table 17 accuracy mismatch weaken reporting, but these drawbacks do not outweigh the substantive improvement in validation.
